draft.title: Person perception
card: Person perception is the process of forming an impression of another person. We often do it within seconds of meeting them.
We build the impression from cues. These include appearance, body language, tone of voice and what the person says or does.
We also use what we already believe, such as past experiences and expectations. Two people can see the same person and form different impressions.
Quick impressions are fast and often useful, but they are based on limited information. They can be wrong.
draft.remember: Person perception is a fast impression built from cues and from what we already believe, so it can be wrong.

a.q: Jai meets a new classmate and decides she is friendly after a few seconds, because she smiles and faces him. What is Jai doing?
opts: Forming an impression from body language cues
Testing his impression against detailed evidence
Explaining her behaviour by her situation
Acting unfairly toward her because of her group
a.why: Jai uses a smile and body position, which are cues, to form a quick impression of a person. He has not gathered detailed evidence. He is also not explaining why she acts as she does, or treating her unfairly.
a.clue: Think about which cues he used and how fast he judged.

b.q: Two students watch the same new teacher walk in. One thinks she seems strict and the other thinks she seems relaxed. Which best explains the different impressions?
opts: Each student's existing beliefs shape how they read the cues
One student saw cues that the other student could not see
Impressions only form after weeks of knowing someone
The teacher's appearance alone decides every impression
b.why: People bring their own past experiences and expectations to the cues they see, so the same person can create different impressions. The cues are shared here, and impressions can form within seconds, so the other options do not fit.
b.clue: The teacher is the same for both. What differs about the students?

a.best: Forming an impression from body language cues

b.best: Each student's existing beliefs shape how they read the cues
